newsitem.title: GERMANY: German soldiers demand asylum for Soviet deserters.
newsitem.headline: German soldiers demand asylum for Soviet deserters.

text.p: Germany's soldiers asked Bonn on Tuesday to give residence rights to about 600 of their former Cold War foes -- deserters from the former Soviet Army in East Germany facing imminent repatriation and probable jail terms.

"The deportation of these young soldiers would be a blow to human rights, because at home in today's Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) they would face incomparably high punishment and persecution," the chairman of the German Army Association, Colonel Bernhard Gertz, said in a statement.

Parliament's interior affairs committee will soon discuss the fate of the 600 officers who deserted after 1990 from the Soviet garrison of 340,000 men gradually pulling out of eastern Germany after German unification. The garrison was taken over by Russia after the end of the Soviet Union.
The committee, which been scheduled to discuss the issue on Wednesday, said it now expected to do so on February 26.

The soldiers say Western intelligence officers interrogated them at the Federal Office for Asylum Applications in Nuremberg, when they were applying for political asylum, and told them it would improve their chances of success.
Although it is unlikely that all of the deserters were able to provide much valuable information to Western intelligence, they say any such contact will be seen at home as treason.

Those being returned to Russia, where the bulk of the soldiers came from, say they expect the military justice system there to try them behind closed doors without a civilian lawyer. Others may be deported to Ukraine.
Russian law prescribes a sentence of up to 10 years for desertion and up to 20 years for treason.
The Frankfurt-based International Society for Human Rights (IGFM), campaigning to help the deserters, says that contrary to Bonn's assertions, both Kiev and Moscow are keen to prosecute.
It says at least two deserters have already been deported, and that others were abducted from German territory by KGB snatchers before the troops pulled out, and are in prison camps.
But for the German government, desertion alone is not a reason for political asylum to be given, nor is mere contact with Western intelligence services.
In a statement last month, it said deserters were told who was questioning them, that they were free not to cooperate, and that their answers would not influence their asylum requests.
Bonn also says it has no evidence that any measures have been taken in Russia against deserters.

It says 63 deserters and 55 family members have been given asylum, and 1,025 rejected, and that each application is assessed for likely persecution at home or the threat of inhumane treatment, execution or torture.
